chapter.title: Apostrophes
chapter.description: Master the rules for using apostrophes correctly to show possession, form contractions, and avoid common errors like confusing possessive pronouns with contractions.

rules.title: Possession with Singular Nouns
rules.explanation: Add an apostrophe and an 's' ('s) to singular nouns to show possession, even if the noun ends in 's' (e.g., Charles's book, boss's desk).

rules.title: Possession with Plural Nouns
rules.explanation: Add only an apostrophe (') to plural nouns that end in 's'. For irregular plural nouns that do not end in 's', add an apostrophe and an 's' ('s).
rules.example: The dogs' bones / The children's toys

rules.title: Contractions
rules.explanation: Use an apostrophe to indicate omitted letters in a contraction.
rules.example: do not -> don't / it is -> it's / who is -> who's

rules.title: Possessive Pronouns vs. Contractions
rules.explanation: Possessive pronouns (its, whose, your, their) NEVER take an apostrophe. Apostrophes in these words indicate a contraction (it's = it is, who's = who is, you're = you are, they're = they are).
rules.example: The cat licked its paw. / It's time to go.

rules.title: Joint vs. Separate Possession
rules.explanation: When two or more people own something jointly, add an apostrophe only to the last owner. If they own items separately, add an apostrophe to each owner.
rules.example: Ben and Jerry's ice cream (joint) / Mark's and Sarah's cars (separate)

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The dog licked its paw after the long walk.
The dog licked it's paw after the long walk.
questions.answer: The dog licked its paw after the long walk.
questions.explanation: 'Its' is a possessive pronoun and does not use an apostrophe. 'It's' means 'it is'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: All of the students' grades improved this semester.
All of the student's grades improved this semester.
questions.answer: All of the students' grades improved this semester.
questions.explanation: Since 'students' is a plural noun ending in 's', the apostrophe goes after the 's' to show plural possession.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The women's locker room was renovated last week.
The womens' locker room was renovated last week.
questions.answer: The women's locker room was renovated last week.
questions.explanation: 'Women' is an irregular plural noun that does not end in 's', so you add ''s' to show possession.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Who's jacket is this left on the chair?
Whose jacket is this left on the chair?
questions.answer: Whose jacket is this left on the chair?
questions.explanation: 'Whose' indicates possession. 'Who's' is a contraction meaning 'who is' or 'who has'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: You're going to love the new restaurant in town.
Your going to love the new restaurant in town.
questions.answer: You're going to love the new restaurant in town.
questions.explanation: 'You're' is the contraction for 'you are'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The girls' coats were hung in the closet.
The girl's coats were hung in the closet.
questions.answer: The girls' coats were hung in the closet.
questions.explanation: Plural possession for regular nouns ending in 's' requires the apostrophe after the 's'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: It's a long way to the top if you wanna rock 'n' roll.
Its a long way to the top if you wanna rock 'n' roll.
questions.answer: It's a long way to the top if you wanna rock 'n' roll.
questions.explanation: 'It's' stands for 'it is'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My boss's office is at the end of the hall.
My boss' office is at the end of the hall.
questions.answer: My boss's office is at the end of the hall.
questions.explanation: Singular common nouns ending in 's' take ''s' to form the possessive.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We saw the Smith's at the grocery store.
We saw the Smiths at the grocery store.
questions.answer: We saw the Smiths at the grocery store.
questions.explanation: Simple plurals of proper names do not require an apostrophe.

questions.question: Choose the sentence in which apostrophes are used correctly.
options: The team's bus arrived early, but the players' equipment was late.
The teams bus arrived early, but the player's equipment was late.
questions.answer: The team's bus arrived early, but the players' equipment was late.
questions.explanation: 'Team' is singular ('team's bus') and 'players' is plural ('players' equipment').

questions.question: Choose the correct usage of the apostrophe.
options: The company revised its policy on remote work.
The company revised it's policy on remote work.
questions.answer: The company revised its policy on remote work.
questions.explanation: 'Its' is the possessive form of 'it'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence with correct possessive punctuation.
options: Jack and Jill's pail was filled with water.
Jack's and Jill's pail was filled with water.
questions.answer: Jack and Jill's pail was filled with water.
questions.explanation: When two people share joint ownership of a single object, the apostrophe goes only on the second name.

questions.question: Choose the sentence with correct possessive punctuation.
options: Tom's and Jerry's ideas were completely different.
Tom and Jerry's ideas were completely different.
questions.answer: Tom's and Jerry's ideas were completely different.
questions.explanation: When two individuals have separate, individual ideas (separate ownership), both nouns take an apostrophe.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The 1980s were famous for neon fashion.
The 1980's were famous for neon fashion.
questions.answer: The 1980s were famous for neon fashion.
questions.explanation: Plural decades do not require an apostrophe before the 's'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She earned straight A's on her report card.
She earned straight As on her report card.
questions.answer: She earned straight A's on her report card.
questions.explanation: Apostrophes are used to form the plural of single letters to avoid confusion (e.g., 'A's' vs 'As').

options: Peter's
Peters'
Peters
questions.answer: Peter's
questions.explanation: Add ''s' to a singular person's name to show possession.

options: children's
childrens'
childrens
questions.answer: children's
questions.explanation: 'Children' is an irregular plural, so add ''s' for possession.

questions.sentence: The ________ (teachers) room is at the end of the corridor.
options: teachers'
teacher's
teachers
questions.answer: teachers'
questions.explanation: If referring to the room used by multiple teachers, put the apostrophe after the plural 's'.

questions.sentence: My ________ (sister) friend is staying with us.
options: sister's
sisters'
sisters
questions.answer: sister's
questions.explanation: Referring to one sister requires 'sister's'.

options: parents'
parent's
parents
questions.answer: parents'
questions.explanation: 'Parents' is a plural noun ending in 's', so the apostrophe follows the 's'.
